questions.question: What is component scanning in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot component scanning explained
questions.direct_answer: Component scanning is Spring's way of finding candidate classes in selected classpath packages and registering bean definitions for them. In a Spring Boot application, @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan, so the default search begins in the application class's package and continues through its subpackages. It detects @Component and annotations built on it, such as @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController, and @Configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how Spring discovers and registers beans automatically without explicit XML or Java configuration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Explaining component scanning as just 'finding classes' without mentioning bean registration or the ApplicationContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan by default, and explain the package scanning root.

sections.title: How Component Scanning Works
sections.content:
Component scanning saves you from registering every application class by hand. During startup, Spring examines class metadata in the configured base packages. When a class matches a scan filter—normally because it has `@Component` or an annotation built on `@Component`—Spring adds a bean definition to the `ApplicationContext`. The container can then create the object, inject its dependencies, and manage its scope and lifecycle.

`@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` are specialised component annotations. `@RestController` is built on `@Controller`, and `@Configuration` is also a component. The names describe the role of each class while still making it discoverable.

**Bookstore example.** If `BookstoreApplication` is in `com.example.bookstore`, an `@Service` in `com.example.bookstore.catalog` is inside the default scan tree. Spring registers that service, registers a controller in `com.example.bookstore.web`, and can pass the service into the controller's constructor.

Scanning is only one way to register beans. `@Bean`, `@Import`, and Boot auto-configuration can register them too. JPA entity discovery and Spring Data repository discovery have separate settings, so widening component scanning does not automatically widen those searches.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Component scanning is the Spring feature that searches selected classpath packages for component classes and registers bean definitions for them. The normal candidates are classes marked with `@Component` or a specialised stereotype such as `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, `@RestController`, or `@Configuration`. Once their definitions are in the `ApplicationContext`, Spring can create the objects and inject their dependencies.

In a Boot application, `@SpringBootApplication` already includes component scanning. If `BookstoreApplication` is in `com.example.bookstore`, a `BookService` under `com.example.bookstore.catalog` and a `BookController` under `com.example.bookstore.web` are both found. When Spring creates the controller, it can supply the scanned service through the constructor.

The boundary is important: Spring does not scan every package in the project by default, and scanning is not the only source of beans. `@Bean`, imports, and auto-configuration can also register beans. Entity and Spring Data repository discovery are separate. I keep the application class in a named root package so the default scan is broad enough for application code without searching unrelated libraries.

sections.title: Component Scanning in a Bookstore Application
When Component Scanning Applies
sections.content:
Use component scanning for application classes that naturally belong to the container, such as controllers, services, repositories, configuration classes, and adapters. Keep the application class above those packages so Boot's default is enough.

For an external library, first use the integration it intentionally exposes—often Boot auto-configuration, an `@Import`, or a documented configuration class. Scanning a library's whole internal package can register classes the library did not mean to expose. Add an explicit scan root only when that package is deliberately designed for component scanning.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the unnamed default package**: it does not mean 'scan nothing'. Boot warns against it because annotations such as `@ComponentScan` can cause every class from every JAR to be read. Put the application in a named root package.
- **Placing a component beside the root**: `com.example.shared` is not below `com.example.bookstore`, so the default bookstore scan does not include it.
- **Expecting one scan to do every job**: changing component scan packages does not change JPA entity scanning or Spring Data repository scanning.
- **Stacking stereotype annotations**: `@Service` and `@Repository` already act as components; adding `@Component` again adds no discovery benefit.

questions.question: What is the default component scan base package in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Default component scan package in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The default component scan base package is the package of the class annotated with @SpringBootApplication. Spring also includes every subpackage below it. For example, an application class in com.example.bookstore includes com.example.bookstore.service, but not the sibling package com.example.shared. The rule follows Java package names and the runtime classpath, not Maven or Gradle module boundaries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the component scan root and can troubleshoot common 'bean not found' issues caused by package structure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring scans the entire project or all com.example packages, not realizing it's anchored to the main class package.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan, and mention how to override the base packages if needed.

sections.title: Where the Default Search Begins
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan`. When no scan packages are supplied, the package of the annotated application class becomes the base package. Spring looks in that package and every package below it.

Suppose `BookstoreApplication` is declared in `com.example.bookstore`. A service in `com.example.bookstore.catalog` is below the base package and can be discovered. A class in `com.example.shared` is a sibling, not a child, so it is outside this scan. The source folder may place both classes near each other, but Java package names—not visual folder distance—decide the relationship.

A Maven or Gradle module is not automatically a scan boundary. A class from another module can be scanned when its JAR is on the runtime classpath and its package is under a configured base. Conversely, a class in the same module is skipped when its package is outside every base.

The unnamed default package is not a useful way to make the base wider. Boot recommends avoiding it because scan annotations can then read classes from every JAR. A named root package gives the application a clear and predictable boundary.

BookstoreApplication"] ROOT --> WEB["com.example.bookstore.web

sibling package"] -. "outside the default base" .-> ROOT ```

sections.title: Which Packages Are Included?
sections.content:
| Class package | Included by the default? | Reason |
|---|---:|---|
| `com.example.bookstore` | Yes | It is the base package. |
| `com.example.bookstore.web` | Yes | It is below the base. |
| `com.example.bookstore.service.pricing` | Yes | Deeper descendants are still below the base. |
| `com.example.shared` | No | It is a sibling of `bookstore`. |
| `org.vendor.client` | No | It is a different package root unless explicitly included. |

sections.title: When the Default Is Enough
sections.content:
The default is enough when the application's component packages share one parent package and the application class sits in that parent. This works for package-by-layer structures such as `web`, `service`, and `repository`, and for package-by-feature structures such as `orders`, `catalog`, and `customers`.

It can also work across several build modules. The required JARs must be on the runtime classpath, and their component packages must still be below the base package. Configure another scan base only when the packages genuinely have different roots; do not add scanning merely because code is stored in another module.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the source folder is the base**: `src/main/java` is not a Java package. Spring follows declared package names.
- **Using the unnamed default package**: Boot warns that this can make scan annotations read every class from every JAR; it does not mean that no beans are found.
- **Treating every module as a separate scan**: modules affect the classpath. They do not each receive a scan root unless configuration creates one.
- **Fixing a missing entity with component scan**: entity and Spring Data repository discovery use separate configuration.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The default component scan base is the package containing the `@SpringBootApplication` class. Spring includes that package and every subpackage below it. It does not use the whole source folder as the base.

For example, if `BookstoreApplication` is in `com.example.bookstore`, Spring can find components in `com.example.bookstore.web` and `com.example.bookstore.service.pricing`. It does not find a component in the sibling package `com.example.shared` unless another scan base or import includes it.

This rule also explains how I debug a missing bean. I first confirm that the class has a component stereotype, then compare its declared package with the application package, and finally check that its JAR is on the runtime classpath. A separate Maven module is not automatically excluded; package position and classpath availability are what matter. I also avoid the unnamed default package because Boot warns that it can make scanning unnecessarily broad.

questions.question: How do you configure component scanning to include additional packages?
questions.title: Configuring @ComponentScan base packages
questions.direct_answer: In a Spring Boot application, set scanBasePackageClasses on @SpringBootApplication and list one marker type for each package root. Include the application class as one marker if its package must remain in the scan. scanBasePackages is the string-based alternative. These settings change component scanning only; use @EntityScan or the relevant @Enable...Repositories annotation for entity and repository packages.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to configure Spring when the default package structure doesn't fit the project needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about @ComponentScan at all, or suggesting moving all code into one package instead of configuring the scan.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention basePackageClasses as the type-safe alternative to string-based basePackages configuration.

sections.title: Configure More Than One Scan Root
sections.content:
A Boot application can set component scan roots directly on `@SpringBootApplication`. The `scanBasePackages` attribute accepts package-name strings. The `scanBasePackageClasses` attribute accepts classes and scans the package of each class; Spring's API recommends it as the type-safe alternative. A small marker interface is useful when no real class should carry this configuration role.

Setting these attributes supplies the scan roots—it does not mean 'keep the default and add one more'. Include `BookstoreApplication.class` as well as `SharedComponents.class` when both package trees must be searched. A string typo may leave a package unscanned without a compiler error; a marker-class reference follows Java refactoring and is compiler checked.

These attributes are aliases for `@ComponentScan` package settings. They do not affect JPA entity discovery or Spring Data repository discovery. Use `@EntityScan` and the matching `@Enable...Repositories` annotation when those package roots also need to change.

Before scanning a third-party library, check its documented integration. A well-designed Boot library often exposes auto-configuration or an importable configuration class. That is a clearer contract than scanning all of the library's internal packages.

sections.title: Configuring Additional Component Scan Packages
When to Configure Additional Scan Packages
sections.content:
Configure extra roots when application-owned components intentionally live under unrelated package names—for example, `com.example.bookstore` and `com.example.shared`. This often appears in older code or in a shared module, but the reason is the package layout, not the module count.

If you control a new application's package design, one clear parent package is usually simpler. For a library, prefer its documented auto-configuration or `@Import` entry point. Use broad component scanning only when the package is an intentional public scan surface.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Leaving out the application root**: configured roots replace the implicit package choice, so list the application class as a marker when its package must still be scanned.
- **Using unchecked strings**: a misspelled package can produce missing beans only at startup. Marker classes make refactoring and spelling compiler checked.
- **Scanning a very broad root**: this can inspect unrelated library classes and may register unwanted candidates or cause naming conflicts.
- **Expecting entities to follow**: `scanBasePackages` and `scanBasePackageClasses` do not configure JPA entity or Spring Data repository scanning.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In a Boot application, I configure extra component scan roots with `scanBasePackageClasses` on `@SpringBootApplication`. Each supplied class acts as a marker for its package. I include the application class as one marker and add a marker interface from every other package tree that must be searched.

For example, I list `BookstoreApplication` and `SharedComponents` as the two package markers. Spring scans the package containing each class and all of its subpackages. The alternative is `scanBasePackages` with package-name strings, but class markers are safer because the compiler and refactoring tools can follow them.

The supplied roots take the place of the implicit default, so forgetting the application root can make existing beans disappear. This setting also applies only to component scanning. If entities or Spring Data repositories live elsewhere, I configure those searches separately. For third-party code, I first look for its auto-configuration or documented import instead of scanning a broad internal package.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
questions.title: @Component vs @Bean in Spring
questions.direct_answer: The difference is where the bean definition comes from: @Component marks a class that component scanning can discover, while @Bean marks a factory method and registers the object returned by that method. Use @Component for a class that naturally identifies itself as an application component; use @Bean when construction must be written explicitly, especially for a library type or a specially configured instance. Both results are Spring-managed beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's two distinct bean registration mechanisms and when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two or not realizing @Bean gives you programmatic control over instantiation and configuration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Bean methods can accept dependencies as parameters and return library or application types, while @Component describes a class that should be discovered by scanning.

sections.title: Two Ways to Register a Bean
sections.content:
`@Component` is placed on a class. If that class is inside a component scan, Spring creates a bean definition for it. `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` are more specific component stereotypes and are normally better when one of those roles fits.

`@Bean` is placed on a factory method, usually inside a `@Configuration` class. Spring calls the method when it needs the bean and registers the returned object. Other beans can be passed into the method as parameters, and annotations such as `@Qualifier`, `@Primary`, and `@Scope` can describe the produced bean.

Both paths end in the same container. The bean can be injected, scoped, proxied, and given lifecycle callbacks. The difference is discovery versus explicit construction—not managed versus unmanaged.

**Order example.** `ReceiptService` is application code with a clear service role, so `@Service` makes it discoverable. `Clock` comes from the JDK and needs a chosen time zone, so a `@Bean` method returns `Clock.systemUTC()`. The service receives that configured clock through its constructor.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: @Component marks a class for scan-based discovery.
@Bean marks a method whose returned object becomes a bean.
Both produce beans managed by the same Spring container.
Choose @Bean for explicit construction; choose a component stereotype when the class naturally owns that role.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@Component` and `@Bean` both register objects with Spring, but they describe the bean in different places. `@Component` is a class-level stereotype found by component scanning. `@Bean` is a method-level factory declaration; Spring registers the object returned by that method.

For example, I can mark an application-owned `ReceiptService` with `@Service`, which is a specialised component annotation. For a JDK `Clock`, I cannot change the library class and I want UTC explicitly, so I write `@Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }`. Spring can then inject that clock into the scanned service.

I choose based on how construction should be expressed. A component stereotype is concise when the class itself has one clear application role. A `@Bean` method is clearer for third-party types, custom factory logic, or several configured instances of one type. It is not a hard 'our code versus library code' rule, and either approach can produce multiple beans that may need qualifiers.

sections.title: @Component vs @Bean Comparison
sections.content:
| Point | @Component | @Bean |
|---|---|---|
| Placed on | A class | A factory method |
| Registered through | Component scanning | Configuration-class processing |
| Object creation | Spring invokes a suitable constructor | Your method returns the object |
| Common fit | A service, controller, repository, or adapter | A library type or explicitly configured instance |
| Dependencies | Constructor or method injection | Factory-method parameters |
| Final result | A Spring-managed bean | A Spring-managed bean |

sections.title: Using @Component and @Bean Together
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use a component stereotype when the class has a stable application role and can be discovered as a unit—for example, an order service or HTTP controller. Choose the most specific stereotype when it adds meaning.

Use `@Bean` when configuration code must choose how to build the object: selecting a time zone, passing vendor options, calling a builder, or creating named variants. Components can also have complex constructors, and several component classes can implement the same interface, so complexity and multiplicity are not exclusive to `@Bean`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling one annotation 'more managed'**: both paths create bean definitions in the same container.
- **Saying @Bean is required for multiple beans of one type**: several component classes can implement one interface; `@Bean` is simply convenient for several configured instances.
- **Creating an accidental second instance**: if a scanned component already exists, a separate `@Bean` method that constructs the same class creates another bean definition. That may be intentional, but injection then needs clear qualifiers.
- **Hard-coding factory dependencies**: `@Bean` methods can declare other beans as parameters and let Spring resolve them.

questions.question: What is bean scope in Spring and what are the common scopes?
questions.title: Spring bean scopes — singleton vs prototype
questions.direct_answer: A Spring bean scope defines how many instances a bean definition can produce and the context in which those instances are kept. singleton is the default and keeps one instance per bean definition in a Spring container; prototype creates a new instance for each container request. In a web-aware context, request, session, application, and websocket scopes tie an instance to the matching web lifetime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that singleton is the default, what it means, and when you'd need a different scope.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring singleton with the Gang of Four singleton pattern, or not realizing most beans are shared instances.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the thread-safety implication of singleton scope and why stateless design matters for shared beans.

sections.title: Scope Connects a Bean to a Lifetime
sections.content:
A bean definition is a recipe. Its scope tells Spring whether that recipe should return one shared instance, create another instance, or look up an instance attached to a web request, session, application, or WebSocket. Scope belongs to a bean definition, so two definitions for the same Java class can use different scopes.

`singleton` is Spring's default. It means one instance for one bean definition in one Spring container; it does not mean one object for the whole JVM. Services are commonly singleton because their work is held in method-local variables or external stores. A singleton may hold mutable state, but concurrent callers then share it and the code must be deliberately thread-safe.

`prototype` asks the container for a new instance whenever that bean is requested from the container. If a prototype is injected once into a singleton constructor, that resolved object stays in the singleton; Spring does not create a new prototype on every method call. Use `ObjectProvider` or another lookup mechanism when the singleton needs a fresh object repeatedly. Spring performs prototype initialization but does not call configured destruction callbacks for those instances.

Web scopes need a web-aware `ApplicationContext`: `request` keeps one instance for an HTTP request, `session` for an HTTP session, `application` for a `ServletContext`, and `websocket` for a WebSocket session. A scoped proxy or provider lets a longer-lived singleton refer to the instance that belongs to the current web scope.

prototype: a new instance for each request to the container, not for every method call.
request, session, application, and websocket follow web lifetimes.
Spring initializes prototype objects but does not run their configured destruction callbacks.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Bean scope defines how instances are obtained from one Spring bean definition and which context owns their lifetime. The default `singleton` scope keeps one instance for that definition in one Spring container. `prototype` creates a new instance whenever the container resolves or looks up that bean.

The web-aware scopes connect state to web lifetimes: `request` gives one instance per HTTP request, `session` per HTTP session, `application` per `ServletContext`, and `websocket` per WebSocket session. For example, an order service is usually a singleton, while a request-scoped `RequestContext` can hold the current correlation ID.

The main boundary is dependency lifetime. Injecting a prototype directly into a singleton constructor resolves it once, so the singleton keeps that one object. If it needs a fresh prototype for each operation, I inject `ObjectProvider<ReportDraft>` and call `getObject()`. I also remember that Spring initializes prototypes but does not call their configured destruction callbacks. Scope is not a substitute for thread safety: shared mutable fields in a singleton still need safe design.

sections.title: Common Spring Bean Scopes
sections.content:
| Scope | Instance is associated with | Typical example | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `singleton` | One bean definition in one container | Stateless service | Shared callers see the same object. |
| `prototype` | Each container request for the bean | Mutable work object | Direct injection into a singleton happens once. |
| `request` | One HTTP request | Correlation or request context | Requires a web-aware context. |
| `session` | One HTTP session | Server-side session state | Not the same as an authenticated user forever. |
| `application` | One `ServletContext` | Servlet-application state | Differs from singleton when several contexts exist. |
| `websocket` | One WebSocket session | WebSocket conversation state | Available only in a web-aware context. |

sections.title: Declaring Bean Scopes in Spring Boot
Choosing the Right Scope
sections.content:
Choose `singleton` for services that do not keep caller-specific mutable data in fields. Use `prototype` when container-created work objects need independent mutable state, and use a provider when a singleton must obtain them repeatedly.

Choose a web scope only when the data truly belongs to that lifetime. A correlation ID fits `request`; a server-side cart may fit `session`; shared servlet state may fit `application`; conversation state may fit `websocket`. Many REST APIs keep services singleton and carry request data in method arguments, so a narrower scope should solve a real ownership problem rather than act as decoration.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading singleton as one object per JVM**: Spring's singleton is per bean definition and container.
- **Expecting a fresh prototype on every business-method call**: direct constructor injection resolves the prototype once; use a provider for repeated lookup.
- **Treating prototype as a garbage-collection rule**: ordinary Java reachability still controls collection. The special issue is that Spring does not invoke configured destruction callbacks for prototype instances.
- **Putting current-user data in a singleton field**: concurrent requests share that field. Keep request data local or use a correctly scoped dependency.

speakable_v2.hook: Singleton is the default scope, so callers of one bean definition normally share the same managed instance.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A singleton @Service shared across concurrent requests

beats.text: Bean scope decides how many copies of a bean Spring makes and how long each lives. The default is singleton, and singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM. Every injection shares it.
Most beans are stateless services, so sharing one copy saves memory. But some beans hold per-request or per-user state. Scopes let you match a bean's lifetime to how the app uses it.

items: Singleton, the default, gives one shared instance per ApplicationContext.
Prototype hands you a fresh instance on every request for the bean.
Request scope lives for a single HTTP request, while session scope spans one user session.

beats.text: Take a singleton OrderService handling concurrent requests. If it stores currentUser in a mutable field, requests can interfere. Stateless service design is a safe default, while intentional shared state needs proper concurrency control.

questions.question: What is @Autowired and how does Spring resolve which bean to inject?
questions.title: @Autowired and Spring dependency injection
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired is Spring's annotation for a required dependency injection point on a constructor, method, or field. Spring starts with beans assignable to the requested type, uses qualifier metadata to narrow that set, and can prefer one @Primary candidate; a matching injection-point name may be a later fallback. One remaining bean is injected. A required dependency with no match, or an unresolved choice between several matches, fails context creation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's dependency injection resolution mechanism and can troubleshoot ambiguous injection scenarios.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reducing candidate selection to a rigid 'type then field name' rule, or treating @Qualifier only as a bean-name lookup.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that constructor injection is preferred over field injection, and explain why (testability, immutability).

sections.title: How Spring Chooses an Injection Candidate
sections.content:
`@Autowired` marks a constructor, method, or field where Spring should supply dependencies. Constructor injection is usually the clearest form because required collaborators appear in the class API and can be passed directly in a unit test. If a class has one constructor, Spring can use it without an `@Autowired` annotation.

For a single-value dependency, Spring begins with beans assignable to the declared type. Qualifier metadata can narrow that group—for example, `@Qualifier("sandbox")` can select a gateway carrying the same qualifier. If several otherwise suitable candidates remain, one `@Primary` bean can serve as the default. Spring may use a matching field or parameter name as a later fallback when name information is available, but an explicit semantic qualifier is clearer.

With no candidate, a required injection point fails. With several candidates and no clear winner, selection also fails. Startup often reports an `UnsatisfiedDependencyException` whose cause describes a missing bean or a non-unique bean, so the useful diagnostic is usually deeper in the cause chain.

Spring can also inject every matching bean into an array, collection, or map. That is a different request from choosing one bean: ordering annotations can control collection order, while `@Primary` is mainly relevant to a single-valued dependency.

No candidate or several unresolved candidates make a required injection fail.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@Autowired` is Spring's annotation for a dependency injection point. It can be used on a constructor, method, or field, although constructor injection normally makes required dependencies easiest to see and test. When a class has only one constructor, Spring uses it even without the annotation.

To choose one bean, Spring starts with candidates assignable to the requested type. A qualifier on the injection point narrows that group to candidates with matching qualifier metadata. If several suitable beans remain, one `@Primary` bean can be the default. A matching parameter or field name may help as a later fallback, but I prefer a qualifier when the distinction has business meaning.

For example, both `LivePaymentGateway` and `SandboxPaymentGateway` implement `PaymentGateway`. Marking the live bean `@Primary` makes it the normal injection. A constructor parameter annotated `@Qualifier("sandbox")` deliberately requests the sandbox bean. If a required dependency has no candidate, or several remain with no winner, the application context fails to start. I read the full exception cause, then check the type, qualifier, primary marker, component scan, and configuration that registered the beans.

sections.title: Single-Bean Resolution Path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  NEED["Required injection point"] --> TYPE["Find type-compatible beans"]
  TYPE --> QUAL{"Qualifier present?"}
  QUAL -->|Yes| FILTER["Keep qualifier matches"]
  QUAL -->|No| CAND["Keep type matches"]
  FILTER --> COUNT{"How many suitable beans?"}
  CAND --> COUNT
  COUNT -->|One| INJECT["Inject the bean"]
  COUNT -->|None| MISSING["Required dependency fails"]
  COUNT -->|Several| PRIMARY{"One preferred candidate?"}
  PRIMARY -->|Yes| INJECT
  PRIMARY -->|No| NAME{"Usable injection-point name match?"}
  NAME -->|Yes| INJECT
  NAME -->|No| AMBIGUOUS["Ambiguous dependency fails"]
```

sections.title: Dependency Injection with @Autowired
When and How to Use @Autowired
sections.content:
Use constructor injection for required collaborators. It exposes the dependency, supports final fields, and lets a unit test create the class without starting Spring. Use a setter or configuration method when replacement after construction is intentional. Field injection works, but it hides construction requirements and makes plain unit tests harder.

Use a semantic qualifier when several beans have different roles, such as `live` and `sandbox`. Use `@Primary` when one candidate is the normal default. For a genuinely optional or repeated lookup, types such as `Optional` or `ObjectProvider` can express that requirement more clearly than a nullable field.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying Spring simply wires by type and then by name**: qualifiers, primary candidates, priority, candidate flags, and the injection shape all matter. A name match is a fallback, not the whole algorithm.
- **Treating @Qualifier only as a bean-name lookup**: a qualifier is metadata that narrows type-compatible candidates; custom qualifier annotations can express meaning directly.
- **Annotating the only constructor unnecessarily**: one constructor is already used for injection.
- **Fixing ambiguity by renaming a field**: this creates a fragile hidden dependency. Prefer `@Qualifier` or `@Primary` so the choice is explicit.
- **Ignoring the cause chain**: the outer startup exception often wraps the useful missing-bean or non-unique-bean message.

beats.text: @Autowired marks a constructor, method, or field injection point. A class with one constructor does not need the annotation, but candidate resolution follows the same rules.
Dependency injection lets a class declare collaborators while the container supplies matching managed beans. Constructor injection keeps those requirements visible.

Qualifier metadata can narrow the candidate set and @Primary can provide a default.
A name match can be a later fallback; no candidate or unresolved ambiguity makes required injection fail.
